title: Assessments of Acoustic Environments by Emotions – The Application of Emotion Theory in Soundscape
central_proposition: This paper proposes a modified conceptual framework for soundscape assessment that explicitly integrates emotion theory, distinguishing between basic emotions, appraisal, and long-term affective states (mood, attitude, knowledge) to better understand human responses to acoustic environments.

concept_definitions.name: Emotion
concept_definitions.definition: Internal, evanescent, mostly conscious, relational psychological experiences, serving a purpose, short-lived, and distinct from mood and attitude by duration.

concept_definitions.name: Mood
concept_definitions.definition: Longer-lived affective states (hours or days) with more remote and less salient causes compared to emotions.

concept_definitions.name: Attitude
concept_definitions.definition: Stable, long-lasting affective dispositions, less affected by the moment than emotions or mood.

concept_definitions.name: Affect
concept_definitions.definition: Superordinate category encompassing emotion, mood, attitude, personality traits, and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: An acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context.

concept_definitions.name: Appraisal
concept_definitions.definition: Processes by which the significance, meaning, or rewarding/aversive nature of events is evaluated, leading to emotional responses.

concept_definitions.name: Personal emotionality
concept_definitions.definition: A person's inherent emotional predispositions that influence how individuals experience emotions differently.

concept_definitions.name: Pleasure (Valence)
concept_definitions.definition: A fundamental dimension of emotion ranging from displeasure to pleasure, distinct from preference or liking.

concept_definitions.name: Arousal
concept_definitions.definition: A fundamental dimension of emotion ranging from sleepy to excitement.

concept_definitions.name: Eventfulness
concept_definitions.definition: A semantic dimension of soundscape related to auditory order and variation, often found alongside pleasantness.

concept_definitions.name: Affective quality
concept_definitions.definition: A property of the stimulus that refers to its capacity to change our emotional responses, capturing the notion of perceived emotions.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived emotions
concept_definitions.definition: Emotional qualities assigned as an intrinsic property of the stimulus.

concept_definitions.name: Felt emotions
concept_definitions.definition: Emotional experiences elicited within the individual.

concept_definitions.name: Audible safety
concept_definitions.definition: An important cue in environments for warning humans of potential danger, derived from affordances, influencing emotional response and behavior.

argument_structure: The paper begins by reviewing general emotion theory, highlighting its relational, manifest, temporal, and purposeful aspects. It then transitions to soundscape research, discussing how emotion theory, particularly dimensional models (valence, arousal), has been applied. It critiques existing soundscape frameworks for not fully integrating emotion's dynamic and long-term effects, and proposes a modified conceptual framework based on ISO 12913-1 to address these gaps.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Emotions are triggered by environmental stimuli (e.g., soundscapes) and processed through appraisal, which involves evaluating the stimulus's significance, meaning, and adaptive relevance. This appraisal process, influenced by context and personal predispositions, leads to immediate basic emotional responses (e.g., pleasure, arousal). These short-lived emotions, in turn, influence behavioral responses and, over time, contribute to more stable affective states like mood, attitude, and knowledge, which then feed back into future appraisals, creating a continuous loop of interaction between person and environment.

findings.mechanism: Emotions are relational and elicited by specific objects or encounters, making them distinct from mood and attitude.
findings.quote: The experience of an emotion can usually be linked to a specific, defining moment and triggered by a specific object

findings.antecedent: Stimulus significance, meaning, rewarding or aversive nature
findings.mechanism: Events act through their significance, not merely as stimuli, to elicit emotions.
findings.quote: they appear to act through their significance, their meaning, their rewarding or aversive nature

findings.mechanism: Elements of appraisal remain closed to comprehensive cognitive penetration, even if consciously controlled in part.
findings.quote: elements of the appraisal process, such as basic emotions [...] remain closed to comprehensive cognitive penetration

findings.mechanism: Emotion is relational, with response strength tied to stimulus strength, but modulated by individual predispositions.
findings.quote: The magnitude of emotional response an individual experiences is strongly related to the magnitude of emotional stimulus

findings.mechanism: Knowledge about a stimulus' significance contributes to personal meaning, which drives emotional responses.
findings.quote: knowledge about a stimulus' significance to well-being, inherent in the concept of appraisal, contributes to one's personal meaning that also drives emotional responses

findings.mechanism: Emotions are intrinsically linked to physiological responses and can be triggered by all sensory systems.
findings.quote: Emotions can be triggered by all human sensory systems, demonstrating an intrinsic link between emotional and physiological responses
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hume and Ahtamad, 2013; Bradley and Lang, 2000; Choi et al., 2015; Fredrickson and Kahneman, 1993

findings.mechanism: Emotions serve a purpose by preparing organisms for action; emotional stimuli are detected more rapidly and gain easier access to conscious awareness.
findings.quote: emotional stimuli are prioritized in perception, are detected more rapidly, and gain access to conscious awareness more easily than non-emotional stimuli

findings.mechanism: Valence and arousal represent primitive motivational parameters that define a general disposition to approach or avoid stimulation, correlating with brain state and evaluation.
findings.quote: valence and arousal represent primitive motivational parameters that define a general disposition to approach or avoid stimulation

findings.consequent: High relevance for survival and well-being
findings.mechanism: Emotions prepare the organism for action or decision, informing the individual of event nature/importance and motivating focus on relevant considerations.
findings.quote: emotional stimuli and emotional responses represent a special type of input – they both represent high relevance for survival and well-being
findings.empirical_support_cited: Gray and Watson, 2007; Brosch et al., 2010; Clore, 1994

findings.mechanism: Soundscape refers to the perceived acoustic environment, whose character results from the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors, understood in context.
findings.quote: The recognized term soundscape thus refers to the perceived acoustic environment of a place, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors
findings.empirical_support_cited: International Organization for Standardization, 2014; Kang et al., 2016

findings.mechanism: Soundscape research aims to understand how acoustic environments affect human perception, including emotional reactions.
findings.quote: The overarching aim of soundscape research is to understand the relationship of people and their acoustic environment, examining the sounds that people value or oppose

findings.mechanism: Music is intentionally composed to arouse emotions, with listeners decoding 'intended' emotions.
findings.quote: It seems beyond question that music as an auditory event can provoke emotions.

findings.mechanism: Acoustic environments can evoke similar emotions to music/speech, but their effect is more subtle and often unnoticed, as they are rarely explicitly designed to induce emotions.
findings.quote: The effect of acoustic environments on emotions is more subtle and often goes unnoticed. Acoustic environments are rarely explicitly ordered or designed to induce emotions.

findings.mechanism: Soundscape researchers have adopted dimensional models of emotion, finding that pleasantness, eventfulness, and familiarity are basic dimensions of affective qualities attributed to acoustic environments.
findings.quote: Axelsson et al. (2010) intensively studied the affective qualities attributed to acoustic environments and proposed a few basic dimensions of affective qualities for soundscapes that reflect the main features of the circumplex model
findings.empirical_support_cited: Axelsson et al., 2010; Russell et al., 1981

findings.mechanism: These dimensions might reflect evolutionary needs across sensory domains, promoting survival by preferring certain environments and avoiding others.
findings.quote: The first two independent dimensions, pleasantness and eventfulness, might reflect evolutionary needs across sensory domains, promoting survival by preferring certain environments

findings.consequent: Appropriateness (match with personal expectations) and positive affective responses
findings.mechanism: Appropriateness, the level of match between expectation and real-world situation, can influence an individual's positive affective responses. Inappropriate matches lead to negative affective responses.
findings.quote: Appropriateness, the level of match between expectation and real-world situation, can influence an individual's positive affective responses to a situation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Aletta et al., 2016; van den Bosch et al., 2018

findings.mechanism: Aesthetic appreciation is grounded in the relationship between the amount of information of stimuli and people's capacity to process this information, which leads to emotional responses.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: Aesthetic appreciation is grounded in the relationship between the amount of information of stimuli and people's capacity to process this information, which leads to emotional responses.

findings.consequent: Appraisal (driving force) and emotional response (stress, unpleasantness)
findings.mechanism: Audible safety, an important evolutionary cue for warning of danger, influences appraisal. Lack of safety leads to vigilance, stress, and unpleasantness.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: Using an evolutionary perspective, audible safety is an important cue in environments for warning humans of potential danger. Auditory environments that lack considerable audible safety require people to become vigilant and alert, resulting in stress and appraised unpleasantness.
findings.empirical_support_cited: van den Bosch et al., 2018; Gibson, 1979

findings.mechanism: Understanding how a place influences a person emotionally is more important than understanding its acoustical properties alone for soundscape appraisal.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: the understanding of the acoustical properties of a place is far less important than understanding how that place influences a person emotionally.

findings.mechanism: While sound intensity can explain some arousal variance, the relationship with valence is more complex, and classical level indicators explain only a small percentage of total variance, indicating other factors are more important.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: the relationship between a physical intensity of sound and valence looked more complex and that classical level indicators explained only a few percentage points of the total variance.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bradley and Lang, 2007a; Yang et al., 2018

findings.antecedent: Environmental sound-induced emotion and its reporting
findings.consequent: Understanding of duration, memory, and integration heuristics
findings.mechanism: There is a significant lack of systematic investigation into how temporal aspects and cognitive processes like memory distortions influence self-reports of emotions elicited by environmental sounds.
findings.source: EMOTIONS AND THEIR DIMENSIONS IN SOUNDSCAPE RESEARCH
findings.quote: There is still a significant lack of understanding in the role of duration, memory, and integration heuristics on environmental sound-induced emotion and its reporting

findings.mechanism: Beyond component sounds, the emotions elicited by a soundscape are significant features that influence how we experience and process information about the environment.
findings.quote: elicited emotions are significant soundscape features aside the component sounds themselves.

findings.mechanism: Frequently unconsciously elicited basic emotions from a soundscape exert influence on individuals' outcomes without conscious awareness.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: the importance of the frequently unconsciously elicited (basic) emotions by a soundscape, which exert influence on individuals' behavior, well-being, and health without one being aware of it.

findings.antecedent: Initial affective appraisal of a soundscape
findings.consequent: Short-term behavioral responses (e.g., moving away) and longer-term outcomes (e.g., habits, health effects)
findings.mechanism: The appraisal process forms a feedback loop where initial affective responses lead to behaviors, which then influence longer-term outcomes, and these outcomes modify future appraisals.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: the initial affective appraisal of a soundscape influences first short-term behavioral responses (such as moving away from the area), which in turn influence longer-term outcomes (such as habits or health effects).

findings.antecedent: Shifts in mood, attitude, and knowledge (from past experiences)
findings.mechanism: Solidified emotions (mood, attitude, knowledge) from past experiences feed back into and modify future appraisals and responses.
findings.source: WHAT DETERMINES EMOTIONAL RESPONSES TO ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENTS?
findings.quote: The resulting shifts in mood, attitude, and knowledge held by an individual may then modify prospective appraisals, leading to modified responses and so on.

findings.mechanism: While the universal character of emotion applies to the human set of emotions, cultural impact takes place more on the emotion regulation stage.
findings.quote: a cultural impact takes place more on the emotion regulation stage

findings.antecedent: Perceived emotions (assigned intrinsic property of stimulus) vs. felt emotions (elicited within individual)
findings.mechanism: Differences in the determination of emotion dimensions are likely due to the missing distinction between perceived and felt emotions.
findings.quote: Thus, it is likely that differences in the determination of emotion dimensions are due to the missing distinction of perceived emotions (assigned intrinsic property of the stimulus) and felt emotions (elicited emotions within the individual).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kallinen and Ravaja, 2006; Zhang and Kang, 2020

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Systematic investigations are needed on the role of duration, memory, and integration heuristics on environmental sound-induced emotion and its reporting.

Future research should make a methodological distinction between requesting reports related to intrinsically triggered emotions (perceived emotion) and extrinsically triggered emotions (felt emotion).

Further research should be guided by the distinction between different stages of emotion and appraisal, including long-term effects (mood, attitude, knowledge) as proposed in the modified conceptual framework.
Research should investigate how the proposed feedback loop of solidified emotions (mood, attitude, knowledge) influences future appraisals and responses in soundscape contexts.

Studies should explore the specific mechanisms by which 'order and variation' in acoustic environments relate to pleasure and arousal, and identify appropriate acoustic indicators for these mechanisms.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly links soundscape research to general emotion theory, particularly dimensional models (valence, arousal, dominance) and evolutionary theories of emotion (adaptive action, survival).
It connects soundscape perception to cognitive appraisal processes, emphasizing the role of meaning and context.
The paper draws parallels between emotion in music and soundscape, while also highlighting their differences.
It integrates the concept of 'audible safety' from affordance theory (Gibson) into soundscape appraisal.
The proposed framework builds upon and modifies the ISO 12913-1 standard for soundscape, integrating dynamic emotional processes and long-term affective states.
methodological_critiques: The difficulty in identifying the causes of emotions presents a challenge for emotion theory and soundscape research alike.
The irrelevance of duration for reporting summarized affect of longer periods (duration neglect) is frequently discussed, implying that retrospective reports may be biased.
Retrospective biases (recollection, belief-based reconstruction) must be considered when requesting measures of emotion experiences.
There is a significant lack of understanding and systematic investigation into the role of duration, memory, and integration heuristics on environmental sound-induced emotion and its reporting.
Most soundscape research dealing with emotions does not differentiate between basic emotions and appraisal.
Most soundscape research has focused on verbal reporting, with less attention to physiological (re)activity or overt behavior.
A methodological distinction is rarely made between requesting reports related to intrinsically or extrinsically triggered emotions in soundscape studies.
Most soundscape studies on emotion dimensions are based on controlled laboratory experiments, with field surveys rarely conducted.
Acoustical indicators alone do not allow comprehensive prediction of emotional responses without considering the meaning attributed to sounds and situations.
There is a general lack of consensus between researchers regarding the roots and causes of soundscape emotion and appraisal, leading to a comprehensive mixture of models and indicators.
model_structure: The paper proposes a modified conceptual framework (Figure 3) based on ISO 12913-1. It depicts 'Sound sources' leading to an 'Acoustic environment', which is perceived in 'Context'. This leads to 'Basic emotions' and 'Appraisal'. 'Appraisal' directly influences 'Behavioral Responses'. Crucially, the modified framework adds a feedback loop where 'Behavioral Responses' and 'Appraisal' contribute to 'Mood, attitude, knowledge', which then feeds back into 'Appraisal', representing the solidification of emotions into longer-term affective states that influence future perceptions.
limitations: A universal definition of emotion and its nature is currently missing.
An established, comprehensive theory of emotion does not yet exist.
The circumplex model of emotion (e.g., Russell's) may not provide a sufficiently rich account of prototypical emotional episodes (e.g., distinguishing fear from anger).
The small variation in familiarity of soundscapes means this component is of limited importance for applied work, though potentially relevant for basic research.
Current studies on soundscape emotion dimensions are still producing results that cannot yet be generalized across all contexts.
Emotional reactions to short sound situations observed in experiments (brief glimpses) cannot simply be attributed to underlying 'motivational states' in real life.
It is not yet possible to establish predictive models of soundscape due to lack of agreement on necessary descriptors.
The exact role of emotion in the context of soundscape has not yet been fully clarified.

paper_metadata.title: Assessments of Acoustic Environments by Emotions – The Application of Emotion Theory in Soundscape
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Assessments of Acoustic Environments by Emotions – The Application of Emotion Theory in Soundscape
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Human beings respond to their immediate environments in a variety of ways, with emotion playing a cardinal role. In evolutionary theories, emotions are thought to prepare an organism for action. The interplay of acoustic environments, emotions, and evolutionary needs are currently subject to discussion in soundscape research. Universal definitions of emotion and its nature are currently missing, but there seems to be a fundamental consensus that emotions are internal, evanescent, mostly conscious, relational, manifest in different forms, and serve a purpose. Research in this area is expanding, particularly in regards to the context-related, affective, and emotional processing of environmental stimuli. A number of studies present ways to determine the nature of emotions elicited by a soundscape and to measure these reliably. Yet the crucial question—which basic and complex emotions are triggered and how they relate to affective appraisal—has still not been conclusively answered. To help frame research on this topic, an overview of the theoretical background is presented that applies emotion theory to soundscape. Two latent fundamental dimensions are often found at the center of theoretical concepts of emotion: valence and arousal. These established universal dimensions can also be applied in the context of emotions that are elicited by soundscapes. Another, and perhaps more familiar, parallel is found between emotion and music. However, acoustic environments are more subtle than musical arrangements, rarely applying the compositional and artistic considerations frequently used in music. That said, the measurement of emotion in the context of soundscape studies is only of additional value if some fundamental inquiries are sufficiently answered: To what extent does the reporting act itself alter emotional responses? Are all important affective qualities consciously accessible and directly measurable by self-reports? How can emotion related to the environment be separated from affective predisposition? By means of a conceptual analysis of relevant soundscape publications, the consensus and conflicts on these fundamental questions in the light of soundscape theory are highlighted and needed research actions are framed. The overview closes with a proposed modification to an existing, standardized framework to include the meaning of emotion in the design of soundscapes.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Emotional responses to soundscapes are mediated by cognitive appraisals of acoustic features and their personal significance.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Circumplex Models of Affect (e.g., PAD model)
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Emotional experiences elicited by soundscapes can be effectively described using dimensional models such as pleasure, arousal, and dominance.
While basic emotions can be identified in response to soundscapes, a comprehensive understanding requires considering more nuanced appraisal and dimensional approaches.

mechanism_chain.description: Causal mechanism connecting acoustic features of a soundscape to the experience of emotion through perceptual processing and cognitive appraisal.

steps.from_construct: Acoustic features of soundscape (e.g., loudness, timbre, semantic content)
steps.to_construct: Perceptual processing of sounds (e.g., auditory scene analysis, sound source identification)
Cognitive appraisal of soundscape (e.g., evaluation of pleasantness, event significance, coping potential)
Activation of emotional response systems (e.g., physiological changes, neural activity)

instruments_used.name: Semantic Differential Scales
instruments_used.construct: perceived soundscape quality, emotional valence, arousal
instruments_used.description: Bipolar adjective scales (e.g., pleasant-unpleasant, calm-agitated) used to rate subjective experiences of soundscapes and associated emotions.

instruments_used.name: Geneva Emotion Wheel (GEW)
instruments_used.description: A visual self-report tool allowing participants to select and rate the intensity of various discrete emotions.

instruments_used.name: Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) / PAD scales
instruments_used.description: Non-verbal pictorial scales used to assess emotional dimensions of pleasure, arousal, and dominance.

stimulus_images.description: Diagram illustrating the proposed conceptual framework for understanding emotional responses to soundscapes, integrating acoustic features, cognitive appraisals, and emotion theories.
